hints: Write out the carbon skeleton of $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH=CHCH}_3$ and find the longest chain that contains the $\text{C=C}$ bond.
walkthrough:
Find the parent chain through the double bond**
Count through the $\text{C=C}$. The chain is $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3$. That is 6 carbons long including the double bond, so the parent is hexene.

Number to give the double bond the lowest number**
Number from the right end so the $\text{C=C}$ starts at carbon 2. That gives hex-2-ene. The methyl branch is then on carbon 4. Put them together as 4-methylhex-2-ene.

hints: Think what stays the same and what changes: connectivity versus arrangement in space.
walkthrough:
Separate connectivity from geometry**
Stereoisomers are not structural isomers. The atoms are joined in the same order, so they have the same structural formula. What is different is how those groups point in space, because rotation is restricted around $\text{C=C}$ or at a chiral centre.
Final answer: Compounds with the same structural formula but with a different arrangement of atoms or groups in space.

hints: Check the two carbons of the $\text{C=C}$ in 4-methylhex-2-ene separately for two different groups on each carbon.
Look away from the double bond at carbon 4 and test whether it is bonded to four different groups.
Recall how one $\text{C=C}$ capable of cis-trans isomerism contributes two isomers, and how one chiral centre contributes two optical isomers.
Combine the two independent sources of stereoisomerism multiplicatively to get the total.
walkthrough:
Test the double bond for cis-trans isomerism**
Look at $\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$ part more fully: left $\text{C}$ has $\text{H}$ and $\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, right $\text{C}$ has $\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_3$. Each doubly bonded carbon carries two different groups and rotation is restricted, so cis-trans (E-Z) isomerism is possible. That alone gives 2 isomers.

Test for a chiral centre**
Now look at C4, the $\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}$ carbon. It is bonded to $\text{H}$, $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH=CHCH}_3$. Those are four different groups, so C4 is chiral (asymmetric). One chiral centre gives a pair of enantiomers, optical isomers.

Multiply the independent possibilities**
The alkene geometry and the chirality are independent. So 2 geometries x 2 optical forms = 4 stereoisomers in total.

Final answer: 4 stereoisomers in total.
Cis-trans (E-Z) isomerism about the C=C double bond because there are two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon.
Optical isomerism due to one chiral carbon centre at C4, bonded to four different groups.

hints: Count the longest chain through $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C=C(CH}_3\text{)}_2$ and place the double bond and methyl branches.
walkthrough:
Name this symmetrical alkene**
The longest chain through the $\text{C=C}$ is 4 carbons, so but-2-ene. There is a methyl group on C2 and another on C3. So the name is 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene.

hints: Recall what cold, dilute, acidified $\text{MnO}_4^-$ does to a $\text{C=C}$ bond without breaking the carbon skeleton.
walkthrough:
Add two OH groups across the double bond**
Cold, dilute manganate(VII) gives mild oxidation, hydroxylation. The $\text{C=C}$ becomes $\text{C-C}$ with an $\text{OH}$ added to each carbon. So $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C=C(CH}_3\text{)}_2$ becomes $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C(OH)-C(OH)(CH}_3\text{)}_2$. In skeletal form draw a C-C backbone with OH on each central carbon.

Final answer: 2,3-dimethylbutane-2,3-diol: $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C(OH)-C(OH)(CH}_3\text{)}_2$. Skeletal formula shows two joined central carbons each bonded to an $\text{OH}$ group and two $\text{CH}_3$ groups.

hints: Think what happens when hot, concentrated $\text{MnO}_4^-$ cleaves the $\text{C=C}$ in $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C=C(CH}_3\text{)}_2$ completely.
walkthrough:
Cleave the double bond to carbonyls**
Hot, concentrated, acidified manganate(VII) breaks the $\text{C=C}$ entirely. Each $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C=}$ fragment becomes $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C=O}$. That molecule is propanone. Two moles of propanone form per mole of alkene.
Final answer: Propanone, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C=O}$

hints: Open the $\text{C=C}$ to a $\text{C-C}$ single bond and join many monomers head to tail, then show three linked repeats.
walkthrough:
Build the addition polymer**
Addition polymerisation simply opens the $\pi$ bond. Each monomer $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C=C(CH}_3\text{)}_2$ becomes a repeat unit $\text{-C(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{-C(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{-}$. Join three of these in a chain, showing the backbone C-C single bonds, four $\text{CH}_3$ groups per repeat, and continuation bonds through the ends.

Final answer: $\text{-[C(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{-C(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{-C(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{-C(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{-C(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{-C(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{-]}_n$ shown as three repeat units of $\text{-C(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{-C(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{-}$ with continuation bonds at each end.

hints: Find the longest chain containing $\text{C=C}$ in $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C=CH}_2$ and number to give the double bond the lowest locant.
walkthrough:
Name the three carbon alkene**
The longest chain is 3 carbons with the double bond starting at C1, so prop-1-ene. There is a methyl branch on C2, giving 2-methylprop-1-ene.
Final answer: 2-methylprop-1-ene (methylpropene also accepted)

hints: Start by polarising $\text{H-Br}$ as $\text{H}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ and think which species the electron rich $\text{C=C}$ will attack.
Draw the first curly arrow from the $\pi$ bond to $\text{H}^{\delta+}$ and a second arrow from the $\text{H-Br}$ bond onto Br.
Decide which carbocation forms when H adds to the $\text{CH}_2$ end versus the $\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_2$ end, keeping the more stable ion.
Finish by showing attack of $\text{Br}^-$ on the carbocation to give $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{CBr}$.
walkthrough:
Set up the electrophilic attack**
$\text{HBr}$ is polar: $\text{H}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$. The $\text{C=C}$ is electron rich and acts as a nucleophile. Draw a curly arrow from the double bond to the $\text{H}^{\delta+}$, and a curly arrow from the $\text{H-Br}$ bond onto $\text{Br}$ to make $\text{Br}^-$. Include lone pairs, charges and partial charges.

Form the most stable carbocation**
$\text{H}^+$ adds to the $\text{CH}_2$ carbon so the positive charge lands on the more substituted carbon, giving the tertiary ion $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C}^+\text{-CH}_3$, i.e. $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C}^+$. Draw this ion in the box with $\text{Br}^-$ alongside.

Capture the carbocation with bromide**
Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on $\text{Br}^-$ to the $\text{C}^+$. This forms the C-Br bond and gives the product $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{CBr}$, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (labelled 2-bromomethylpropane in the paper).

Final answer: Step 1: $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C=CH}_2 + \text{H}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$; curly arrow from $\text{C=C}$ to $\text{H}^{\delta+}$, curly arrow from $\text{H-Br}$ bond to $\text{Br}^{\delta-}$.
Step 2: tertiary carbocation $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C}^+$ formed plus $\text{Br}^-$.
Step 3: curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{Br}^-$ to $\text{C}^+$ giving $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{CBr}$ (2-bromo-2-methylpropane).

hints: Compare the two possible carbocation intermediates leading to the 2-bromo versus 1-bromo product: tertiary versus primary.
Recall how methyl groups release electrons toward a neighbouring positive charge.
Link greater electron release to lower charge density on $\text{C}^+$ and hence lower activation energy and faster formation.
walkthrough:
Identify the competing intermediates**
If $\text{H}^+$ adds to the $\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_2$ end you get a primary carbocation $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CH-CH}_2^+$. If $\text{H}^+$ adds to the $\text{CH}_2$ end you get the tertiary carbocation $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C}^+$. The product ratio is decided by which ion is more stable.

Use the inductive effect to rank stability**
Alkyl groups push electrons toward the positive centre, the positive inductive effect. The tertiary ion has three electron releasing methyl groups around $\text{C}^+$, the primary ion has only one. More donation spreads and reduces the concentrated positive charge density.

Connect stability to major product**
Lower charge density means lower energy and greater stability. The tertiary ion forms much more readily, so almost all reaction goes via that route, giving 2-bromomethylpropane as the major (Markovnikov) product.

Final answer: The tertiary carbocation leading to 2-bromomethylpropane is more stable than the primary carbocation leading to 1-bromomethylpropane.
This is due to the positive inductive effect / electron donating effect of three methyl groups (compared with one), which reduces the charge density on the $\text{C}^+$.
Hence the tertiary intermediate forms faster and gives the major product.
